idiom_name: trait implementations driven by a runtime (std Future polled by an executor, tower Service, axum Handler)
implementation_notes: Rust hands the inversion to the runtime through traits: std::future::Future is inert until an executor polls it and registers a waker, so the runtime decides when your code continues, while tower::Service and axum::Handler are the contracts servers invoke per request. The classic framework base class becomes a trait implementation (or an async fn the framework accepts), which is the idiomatic shape for services and handlers; hand-written loops are reserved for code that must own scheduling itself. The Rust-specific cost is that ownership and Send bounds are part of the extension contract, so the framework dictates more about your types than callback-based languages do.
pitfalls: Blocking inside poll or an async handler stalls the executor thread; CPU-bound or blocking work must be moved with spawn_blocking or a dedicated pool.
Values held across an await point must be Send and owned for long enough, so captured references in handlers are a frequent source of lifetime and borrow-checker errors.
